presentingComplaint: Bloody diarrhoea up to 10 times a day for 5 days with crampy abdominal pain and fever, on a background of known ulcerative colitis.
history: 27-year-old woman with left-sided ulcerative colitis diagnosed 4 years ago, previously well controlled on mesalazine, presents with a 5-day history of worsening bloody diarrhoea (now 8-10 bowel movements/day, most containing visible blood and mucus), urgency, and tenesmus. She reports crampy lower abdominal pain, subjective fevers, and malaise. She has had poor oral intake for 2 days due to nausea. No recent travel, no antibiotic use, no NSAID use. She stopped her mesalazine 3 weeks ago after running out of medication and has had escalating symptoms since. No prior surgery. No family history of colorectal cancer. No sick contacts. No recent hospitalization.
examination: Ill-looking, mildly dehydrated young woman. Diffuse mild-to-moderate tenderness over the lower abdomen, worse in the left iliac fossa, without guarding, rigidity, or rebound. No abdominal distension. Bowel sounds present. Digital rectal exam reveals fresh blood and mucus. No perianal fistula or abscess. No skin, joint, or eye extra-intestinal manifestations noted on this visit.
imaging: Abdominal X-ray: no evidence of toxic megacolon or free air, no significant colonic dilatation

Flexible sigmoidoscopy (limited, unprepped): diffuse continuous mucosal inflammation with loss of vascular pattern, friability, and superficial ulceration from rectum extending proximally, consistent with active severe colitis
microbiology: Stool microscopy, culture and sensitivity: pending, no pathogens isolated to date
Stool ova, cysts and parasites: negative
finalDiagnosis: Acute severe ulcerative colitis flare (Truelove and Witts criteria met)
contraindications: Avoid anti-motility agents (e.g., loperamide) — risk of precipitating toxic megacolon
Empirical antibiotics not routinely indicated once infection excluded, unless toxic megacolon or perforation suspected
edgeCases: Infectious colitis must be excluded with stool studies (culture, C. difficile toxin, ova/parasites) before committing to escalation of immunosuppression, though treatment should not be delayed pending results if severity criteria are met
Toxic megacolon is a critical complication to actively exclude with serial abdominal exams and imaging; colonic dilatation >6 cm with systemic toxicity changes management urgently toward surgery
Steroid-refractory disease at 72 hours requires rescue therapy (infliximab or ciclosporin) or colectomy discussion
Full colonoscopy is avoided in acute severe flare due to perforation risk; limited unprepped flexible sigmoidoscopy is preferred for initial assessment
